facts.statehood_note: President Thomas Jefferson approved the act accepting Ohio's constitution on February 19, 1803. In 1953 Congress formally confirmed March 1, 1803, as the statehood date. Ohio was the first state made from the Northwest Territory.
facts.nickname: The Buckeye State (also called "the Mother of Presidents")
facts.motto: With God, all things are possible (suggested by a 10-year-old Cincinnati boy in 1958 and adopted in 1959)
borders: Lake Erie (with Ontario, Canada, across the lake)
facts.name_origin: Named for the Ohio River, whose name comes from a Seneca word meaning "good river" or "great river."

government.legislature: Ohio General Assembly ("Legislative power is vested in the General Assembly," Article II, Section 1)
government.chambers: Ohio Senate (33 senators, 4-year terms, limited to two terms in a row) and Ohio House of Representatives (99 representatives, 2-year terms, limited to four terms in a row)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term). The constitution says no one may be governor for more than two 4-year terms in a row.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Ohio (a chief justice and six justices, 7 in all, serving staggered 6-year terms)
government.local: 88 counties. Since 1912 cities and villages have had "home rule," the power to run many of their own affairs.
government.constitution: Ohio's first constitution was written in 1802. The current constitution was written at a convention in 1850 to 1851 and is still in use; in 1912 voters added 34 amendments, including the initiative and referendum, which let citizens propose and vote on laws.
government.kid_line: "All men are, by nature, free and independent, and have certain inalienable rights" (Article I, Section 1, 1851)

long_ago.about: Adena people, living about 1000 to 800 BC and after, built some of the first villages that stayed in one place and grew plants they had tamed. Great Serpent Mound is the best-known site linked to them.
Between about 1,600 and 2,000 years ago, Hopewell people built huge earthen circles, squares, and octagons using a standard unit of measure, and they traded across about a third of the continent.

long_ago.nation: Fort Ancient peoples and the Shawnee
long_ago.about: Fort Ancient communities lived in the Ohio Valley for hundreds of years, and the Shawnee likely descend from them. Many Shawnee left Ohio in the 1600s because of Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) attacks and returned in the 1700s.
The Wyandot once lived on Georgian Bay in Ontario, fled Haudenosaunee raids in the mid-1600s, and settled on the south shore of Lake Erie in the 1720s.
These nations also had towns in Ohio. The Miami town of Kekionga was a major trading center, and Mingo (Seneca) towns stood on the Cuyahoga River.

first_peoples.today_note: No federally recognized tribe is listed as based in Ohio today. The Ohio History Connection lists 18 federally recognized nations with historic ties to Ohio, such as the Shawnee Tribe, Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma, Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma, Wyandotte Nation, Seneca-Cayuga Nation, Delaware Nation, Delaware Tribe of Indians, Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, and Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma. Many are in Oklahoma today. After removal treaties forced them west, most had to move again, and an 1867 treaty created new homelands in northeastern Oklahoma and southeastern Missouri.
sites: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since September 19, 2023 (Mound City Group and four other sites in Hopewell Culture National Historical Park, Octagon and Great Circle Earthworks in Newark, and Fort Ancient Earthworks in Oregonia)
Newark Earthworks, Ohio's official state prehistoric monument
John Rankin House and John P. Parker House in Ripley, on the Ohio River (Underground Railroad)

history.event: Adena people build early villages and grow plants in the Ohio Valley.
Hopewell people build giant earthworks and trade over a huge area of North America.
Fort Ancient communities fade, and Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) wars push the Shawnee out of Ohio for a time. In the 1700s the Shawnee return and the Wyandot settle near Lake Erie.
At Gnadenhutten, Pennsylvania militiamen murder 96 peaceful Christian Lenape men, women, and children.
The Northwest Ordinance creates the Northwest Territory, which includes Ohio, and bans slavery there.
In the Treaty of Greenville, the nations of the Western Confederacy are forced to give up much of present-day Ohio.
Ohio becomes the 17th state, the first made from the Northwest Territory.
In the War of 1812, Oliver Hazard Perry wins the Battle of Lake Erie. The Shawnee leader Tecumseh, who fought for the British, is killed at the Battle of the Thames.
In Ripley, the Rankin family shelters hundreds of freedom seekers who cross the Ohio River from Kentucky. A lit candle in their window could be seen across the river.

The Shawnee-Seneca Mixed Band of about 300 people at Lewistown is made to sign away its land and move west. The U.S. does not pay all the money it promised. The Wyandot cede about 114,000 acres in March 1842; in 1843 their chiefs record the families leaving Ohio for the West.
Ohio adopts its current constitution. In May, Sojourner Truth speaks for the rights of women and Black Americans at the Ohio Women's Rights Convention in Akron.
John Mercer Langston is elected town clerk of Brownhelm Township, one of the first Black Americans elected to public office in the United States.

In the Civil War, Ohio sends more soldiers for its population than any other Union state, and almost 35,000 Ohioans die. Generals Grant, Sherman, and Sheridan are all from Ohio, and John P. Parker's foundry makes iron castings for the Union.

During Reconstruction, Ohio voters in 1867 reject a state constitutional amendment that would have let Black men vote. The Fifteenth Amendment, which Ohio's legislature ratified by a single vote, becomes part of the U.S. Constitution in 1870 and protects Black men's right to vote.

trailblazers.name: Tecumseh
trailblazers.text: Tecumseh was born in the Ohio country around 1768 (an Ohio historical marker near Xenia marks a traditional birthplace). Around 1809 he led renewed Shawnee resistance to American expansion, which led to Tecumseh's War. He fought on the British side in the War of 1812 and was killed at the Battle of the Thames in 1813; after his death most Shawnee were forced out of Ohio.

trailblazers.name: John P. Parker
trailblazers.group: Black American inventor and Underground Railroad conductor
trailblazers.text: Once enslaved himself, Parker lived in Ripley and helped freedom seekers cross the Ohio River from Kentucky. He was one of the first African Americans to receive patents for his inventions, and his foundry made iron castings for the Union during the Civil War.

trailblazers.name: Sojourner Truth
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, abolitionist and women's rights speaker
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved as Isabella Baumfree, she spoke Dutch as her first language and won her freedom in 1826. In May 1851 at the Ohio Women's Rights Convention in Akron she gave a famous speech for women's and Black Americans' rights. She could not read or write, so the speech comes to us in two different versions, written down by Marius Robinson (1851) and Frances Dana Gage (1863).

trailblazers.name: John Mercer Langston
trailblazers.group: Black American lawyer, abolitionist, and lawmaker
trailblazers.text: Raised in Ohio, he graduated from Oberlin College and in 1855 was elected town clerk of Brownhelm Township, one of the first Black elected officials in the nation. He helped lead the Ohio Anti-Slavery Society, recruited Black soldiers for the Union, and later founded Howard University's law school.

trailblazers.name: Mary Jane Patterson
trailblazers.text: Mary Jane Patterson was born in Raleigh, North Carolina, and her parents, probably freedom seekers, brought her to Oberlin, Ohio, as a young child. In 1862 she graduated from Oberlin College, the first African American woman to earn a bachelor's degree, and in 1871 she became the first Black principal of the Preparatory High School for Negroes in Washington, D.C.

trailblazers.name: Colonel Charles Young
trailblazers.group: Black American Army officer and educator
trailblazers.text: Born to enslaved parents in Kentucky, he moved with his family to Ripley, Ohio, in 1866. He became the third African American to graduate from West Point (1889), led Buffalo Soldiers, was the first African American superintendent of a national park, and taught at Wilberforce University. His Wilberforce home is now a national monument.

trailblazers.name: Toni Morrison
trailblazers.text: Toni Morrison was born in Lorain, Ohio, in 1931 and became one of America's great novelists. Her novel Beloved won the Pulitzer Prize in 1988, and in 1993 she became the first African American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

landforms: Glaciated till plains covering most of the state
The flat Great Black Swamp region in the northwest
The unglaciated Allegheny Plateau in the southeast, with rugged hills and forests
Campbell Hill (1,549 feet), the highest point
Lake Erie islands such as Kelleys Island, with glacial grooves several feet deep
waters: Lake Erie (312 miles of Ohio shoreline)
Ohio and Erie Canal (1825 to 1832), linking Lake Erie to the Ohio River
geography.regions: Most of Ohio is flat to rolling till plains left by glaciers, with the old Great Black Swamp in the northwest and the hilly, unglaciated Allegheny Plateau in the southeast.

ecosystems.name: Lake Erie
ecosystems.about: Lake Erie is the shallowest and warmest Great Lake and holds about half of all the fish in the Great Lakes, including walleye and yellow perch. Fertilizer washing into streams can feed harmful blue-green algae blooms.

ecosystems.name: Cuyahoga River valley
ecosystems.about: Factory waste and sewage once made the Cuyahoga River catch fire (1952 and 1969). After cleanup, Cuyahoga Valley National Park (2000) is home to beavers, bald eagles, and great blue herons.

ecosystems.name: Ancient Ordovician sea (southwestern Ohio)
ecosystems.about: About 455 to 443 million years ago, a sea covered southwestern Ohio. Its limestone and shale hold fossils of Isotelus, a trilobite that could grow over a foot long.

science.weather: Hot, humid summers and cold winters, with lake-effect snowstorms on Lake Erie's southeast shore. Floods are the biggest danger: the Great Flood of 1913 was Ohio's worst natural disaster, killing at least 428 people. Small earthquakes also happen; the 1937 Anna earthquake (magnitude 5.4) was the strongest known.
science.resources: Farmland, Lake Erie fisheries, and rivers. Ohio has the nation's third-largest manufacturing sector and second-largest automobile production, and more jobs today are in information and services.
science.highlight: Ohio's state fossil, the trilobite Isotelus, was chosen in 1985 after Dayton-area third and fourth graders asked for it. A giant Isotelus found near Dayton in 1919 measures 14.5 by 10.25 inches, one of the largest complete trilobites ever found, and is shown at the Smithsonian.

g3_ss.title: Ohio's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Columbus, the 88 counties, Lake Erie, and the Ohio River; meet the General Assembly (33 senators, 99 representatives), the governor, and the 7-member Supreme Court; read Article I, Section 1.

g3_ss.title: Ohio's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: The Adena and Hopewell earthwork builders, then the Shawnee, Wyandot, Lenape, Miami, and Seneca, and where these nations live today.

g3_ss.title: Ohio Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies of Tecumseh, John P. Parker, Sojourner Truth's Akron speech, John Mercer Langston, Mary Jane Patterson, Charles Young, and Toni Morrison.

g45_ss.title: Ohio's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks (World Heritage, 2023) and Serpent Mound; Shawnee and Wyandot life; Gnadenhutten (1782), the Treaty of Greenville (1795), and removal treaties of 1831 and 1842.

g45_ss.title: The Northwest Territory and Early Ohio
g45_ss.plan: The Northwest Ordinance and its ban on slavery (1787), statehood (1803), Tecumseh and the War of 1812, and the Ohio and Erie Canal.

g45_ss.title: Ohio 1803 to 1877: Freedom's Border
g45_ss.plan: The Underground Railroad at Ripley (Rankin and Parker), the 1851 constitution and Sojourner Truth's speech, Langston's 1855 election, Mary Jane Patterson at Oberlin, Ohio's role in the Civil War, and the 1867 vote and the Fifteenth Amendment during Reconstruction.

g3_sci.title: Trilobite Detectives
g3_sci.plan: What a trilobite was, how fossils form in ancient sea mud, and how Ohio students helped choose Isotelus as the state fossil.

g3_sci.title: Lake Erie Fish
g3_sci.plan: Meet walleye and yellow perch, and learn why a shallow lake is warm and full of fish.

g3_sci.title: Snow from the Lake
g3_sci.plan: How lake-effect snow forms on Lake Erie's southeast shore, with a simple weather-tracking chart.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers Shaped Ohio
g45_sci.plan: Compare glaciated till plains with the unglaciated Allegheny Plateau, and examine the glacial grooves on Kelleys Island.

g45_sci.title: The River That Caught Fire
g45_sci.plan: The Cuyahoga River fires, pollution and cleanup, and the return of beavers, eagles, and herons to Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

g45_sci.title: Floods and Algae Blooms
g45_sci.plan: The Great Flood of 1913, how fertilizer runoff feeds algae blooms in Lake Erie, and what communities do to protect water.
